extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and Interference/Technology Center Practice Specialists); useful to patent practitioners preparing or responding to interference/derivation matters
extracted.subtask_description: MPEP chapter guidance on identifying, suggesting, preparing for, administering, and taking post-decision action for interference (pre‑AIA) and derivation (AIA) proceedings at the USPTO. Focused on examiner procedures, statutory tests, thresholds, and coordination with IPS/Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory basis for interferences (pre-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: An interference is a contest under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 135(a) between an application and either another application or a patent to determine priority (who first invented) within the meaning of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once suggested under 37 CFR 41.202, an administrative patent judge declares the interference and the Board adjudicates priority and patentability questions; final adverse decisions may constitute final refusal or claim cancellation under the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interfering subject matter test (37 CFR 41.203(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: An interference exists if the subject matter of a claim of one party would, if prior art, have anticipated or rendered obvious the subject matter of a claim of the opposing party, and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be construed in light of the application in which they appear for interference purposes. Identical claim language does not guarantee same invention; means-plus-function and differences in corresponding structure can change scope. Numerous examples illustrate species/genus, Markush groups, composition vs genus, and structural equivalence analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count and claim correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'count' is the Board's description of the interfering subject matter that sets the scope of admissible proofs on priority. A claim corresponds to a count if the count, treated as prior art, would have anticipated or rendered obvious the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every count must have at least one corresponding claim for each party; a claim can correspond to more than one count. Examples explain when species/genus claims correspond and when a showing of obviousness is required for correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) to post‑March 16, 2013 applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) applies to every claim in an application if (1) it contains or contained at any time a claimed invention having an effective filing date before March 16, 2013; or (2) it is ever designated a continuation, divisional, or CIP of an application that contained such a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-AIA 102(g) also applies to any patent resulting from such an application. If an application not subject to pre-AIA 102(g) interferes with a patent subject to pre-AIA 102(g), the examiner should consult with an IPS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation with Interference Practice Specialist (IPS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must consult immediately with an Interference Practice Specialist in their Technology Center when a possible interference is identified; IPSs must approve referral of a suggested interference to the Board and sign Form PTO-850.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPSs stay current by consulting with APJs and may arrange APJ consultations. Examiners should promptly address inquiries from IPSs and follow a plan of action developed case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completion of examination before initiating contested case (37 CFR 41.102)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a contested case is initiated, examination (or reexamination) on each involved application and patent must be completed, and there must be at least one claim that is patentable but for a judgment in the contested case and that would be involved in the contested case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference should rarely be suggested until examination is completed on all other issues; pending claims must be allowed, finally rejected, or canceled; appeals and petitions must be decided. Form paragraph 23.01 may acknowledge premature requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issuance and suspension policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowed claims should be issued to the greatest extent possible; suspension of prosecution pending a possible interference should be rare and not entered prior to IPS consultation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two applications claim same patentable invention and one is in condition for allowance while the other is not, the allowed application should generally be issued (but the second applicant may be given a brief opportunity to put their app in condition). When both are in condition for allowance and earliest effective filing dates are within six months, an A v A interference may be suggested; if not within six months, the earlier should issue and the later be rejected over it or required to make a priority showing under 37 CFR 41.202(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice when both applications in condition for allowance
rubrics_metrics.description: When both applications are in condition for allowance, the handling depends on whether earliest effective filing dates are within six months: within six months → application versus application interference may be suggested (subject to 37 CFR 41.202(d)); more than six months → earlier application should issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note interplay with availability as prior art (pre-AIA 102(e)/(a)) and the possibility of requiring a priority showing under 37 CFR 41.202(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-interfering claims treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that does not interfere is directed to a patentably distinct invention and should not be delayed; if an application contains both interfering and non-interfering claims, a restriction should be made between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-interfering claims should ordinarily be issued promptly unless term limited (terminal disclaimer, reissue). If applicant traverses restriction, traversal may be maintained or treated as concession that non-interfering claims correspond to the count; leaving non-interfering claims delays issuance unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction of unpatentable claims to avoid delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Restriction of unpatentable claims may be appropriate when prosecution of the unpatentable claims to completion would unduly delay initiation of an interference and that delay would prejudice another stakeholder (applicant, public).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinarily restricting claims solely because they are not patentable is inappropriate; IPS approval is required before making such a restriction. Examples show broad vs narrow claims and prejudice to other parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue applications and interference (Winter v. Fujita)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue applicants are not permitted to add claims that would not correspond to a count; the Board will not permit reissue applicants to add claims that do not correspond to the count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the burden lies with the reissue applicant to comply with Winter, the examiner need not require restriction of non-interfering claims, but the practice explains why reissue applicants may file multiple reissue applications for the same patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggesting an interference — who suggests matters
rubrics_metrics.description: A suggestion for an interference may come from an applicant or from an examiner; who suggests determines what must be done and shown prior to declaration of an interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In either case the examiner must consult with an IPS, who may then refer the suggested interference to the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference preparation tasks (headings)
rubrics_metrics.description: When preparing an application for interference, tasks include: Interference Search; Obtaining Control Over Involved Files; Translation of Foreign Benefit Application; Sorting Claims; Applicant Suggestion; Identifying the Other Application or Patent; Counts and Corresponding Claims; Explaining Priority; Adequate Written Description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These preparation steps require case-specific actions such as searches to identify potentially interfering subject matter, ensuring control/access to involved files, translating foreign priority documents, sorting and matching claims to counts, and documenting priority and written description support; consult IPS for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold issues that can defeat standing
rubrics_metrics.description: Threshold issues include no interference-in-fact; and, for involved application claims first made after publication/issuance of the movant, repose under 35 U.S.C. 135(b) or unpatentability for lack of written description under 35 U.S.C. 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These threshold issues, if resolved in favor of the movant, would deprive the opponent of standing in the interference and should be scrutinized before declaring an interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description enforcement before declaring interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement of the written description requirement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) receives close scrutiny before an interference is declared to preserve efficiency and integrity of interferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an involved application claim lacks adequate written description, the claim may be found unpatentable before an interference is declared. See examples and precedent (e.g., Berman v. Housey).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling patents with outstanding issues before suggesting interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents undergoing reexamination, reissue, petitions (e.g., late maintenance fee), disclaimers, or corrections ordinarily must have these issues resolved before an interference is suggested because they may affect whether/how an interference may be declared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: an expired patent due to unpaid maintenance fee cannot be in interference unless petition to accept delayed payment is granted; statutory disclaimers or correction of inventorship that remove the 'another inventor' basis preclude an interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference pendency target (37 CFR 41.200(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent interferences shall be administered such that pendency before the Board is normally no more than two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an administrative target for timely resolution at the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel after interference (losing party)
rubrics_metrics.description: A losing party is barred (estopped) from raising an issue it lost during the interference; estoppel includes (1) merits estoppel — barred from seeking a claim that would have been anticipated or obvious by the lost count, and (2) procedural estoppel — barred from seeking relief from the examiner that could have been sought in the interference but was not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should consult IPS before allowing claims added or amended post-interference. Examples illustrate estoppel on identical claims, generic claims that encompass lost subject matter, obviousness-based estoppel, procedural estoppel for not moving/amending during interference, and exceptions where the Board prevented the party from raising the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: No interference-in-fact and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgment of no interference-in-fact means no interference is needed to resolve priority between the parties; neither party has lost the interference for estoppel purposes and such a judgment bars further interference between the same parties for the same subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Board held no interference-in-fact, that holding may not be reopened in further examination; if a later claim by a previously losing party again claims same invention as the count, interfering claims should be rejected as estopped.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office procedure following CAFC decision
rubrics_metrics.description: If the losing party appeals to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit and is unsuccessful with a final mandate, proceedings are considered terminated on the mandate date and the application may not be revived by the USPTO on petition for alleged abandonment resulting from actions taken in proceedings outside the agency (Morganroth v. Quigg).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This governs post-appeal Office procedure regarding revival and finality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation proceeding statutory basis (AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: A derivation proceeding under 35 U.S.C. 135 determines whether an inventor named in an earlier application derived the claimed invention from an inventor named in the petitioner's application and, without authorization, the earlier application was filed; derivation is applicable to AIA first-inventor-to-file applications and patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The petition must set forth with particularity the basis for finding derivation; where standards for instituting are met the Director may institute a derivation proceeding and the Board may correct inventorship where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation definitions and scope (37 CFR 42.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key derivation definitions include: affidavit; Board; business day; confidential information; final; hearing; involved (application/patent/claim that is the subject of the proceeding); judgment; motion; party; petition; petitioner; preliminary proceeding; proceeding; trial; rehearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding these definitions is necessary to determine applicable procedure under part 42 and to differentiate derivation trials from interferences (interferences are administered under part 41).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult Technology Center Practice Specialist (TCPS) for derivation issues
rubrics_metrics.description: When an appropriate petition for derivation has been received by the Board and a notice is entered into the respondent’s file, the examiner should refrain from taking further action until consulting with the Technology Center Practice Specialist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims in the petitioner’s application that are patentably indistinct from respondent’s application or patent should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) and maintained until jurisdiction transfers to the Board; examples include adding a notice to respondent’s file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board assumption of jurisdiction in derivation proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may assume jurisdiction of any involved application, reexamination, reissue, or patent in which a petition for derivation has been filed; when the Board assumes jurisdiction no action by the examiner may be taken until jurisdiction is returned by the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurisdiction may be assumed at any time, including before the application is otherwise in condition for allowance; other Office proceedings are suspended except as the Board orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action after a derivation proceeding is decided
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction returns to the examiner once the derivation proceeding terminates. The examiner must reopen prosecution to consider Board recommendations, enter any recommended rejections, and maintain them unless the applicant overcomes them with amendment or new evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judgment against a claim in derivation finally disposes of the claim; if no claim remains allowable, issue a notice of abandonment. Extraordinary remedies (e.g., changes to inventorship or ownership) may require updating correspondence and should prompt consultation with a TCPS.

rubrics_metrics.name: NASA and Department of Energy ownership contests
rubrics_metrics.description: Ownership of inventions made pursuant to government contracts may be vested in the contracting agency; the Board determines certain ownership contests (e.g., NASA 42 U.S.C. 2457 and DoE 42 U.S.C. 2182) using interference procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants covered by these Acts must file statements regarding conception/making of the invention and relation to the government contract. While not technically interferences, interference practices generally apply; examiner should coordinate with Licensing and Review and IPS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions relevant to interference proof (Accord benefit; Constructive reduction to practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accord benefit: Board recognition that a patent application provides a proper constructive reduction to practice under 35 U.S.C. 102(g)(1). Constructive reduction to practice: a described and enabled anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102(g)(1) in a patent application of the subject matter of a count; earliest constructive reduction to practice is the earliest in a continuous chain of patent applications meeting statutory requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuity of a chain requires compliance with 35 U.S.C. 119-121, 365, or 386 for each subsequent application. These concepts control priority proofs in interferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senior party presumption and involved claim definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior party: party entitled to presumption under § 41.207(a)(1) that it is the prior inventor; junior party: any other party. Involved claim: a claim that has been designated as corresponding to the count for purposes of 35 U.S.C. 135(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senior party has initial presumption of priority; understanding who is senior/junior affects burdens and proofs in interference.
